1000244.etyen:
Borrowed from German Polen (“Poland”), from Middle High German Polen or Polēnen. The German name belongs to the same word family as Pole (“Pole”), ultimately from Old Polish Polanie (“Poles; field dwellers”), from Proto-Slavic *poľane (“Poles; field dwellers”), the plural of *poľaninъ (“field dweller”), itself derived from *poľe (“field”). The latter has tentatively been connected with Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat, wide”).
Compare Polish Polska, Czech Polsko, Slovak Poľsko, Norwegian Nynorsk Polen, Danish Polen, Swedish Polen, Dutch Polen and Luxembourgish Polen (“Poland”).

The Old Latin form is generally derived from Proto-Italic *Māwortis, although an alternative reconstruction *Māmart- has also been proposed; the latter would require an otherwise unusual change of medial *-m-* to *-w-*. Cognate with Oscan 𐌌𐌀𐌌𐌄𐌓𐌔 (mamers, “Mars”), and compare the archaic form Māmartei, attested on the Lapis Satricanus. 1002292.etyen:
Probably a free-standing use of the same intensifying element as ør- (“very, extremely”); compare ørende (“very, extremely”). The prefix ør- continues Old Norse ør- (“out; utterly”), from Proto-Germanic *uz- (“up, out”), from Proto-Indo-European *úd-s (“up, off”), ultimately from *úd (“out, outward”). Already in Old Norse, the prefix had developed an intensifying use meaning “utterly”, especially with adjectives denoting smallness, shortness, poverty or deficiency.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk ør-, Icelandic ör- (“extremely, very”), Old English or- (“out, away”), Old High German ur- (“out, away”)

Probably a calque of Danish De Forenede Nederlande (“the United Netherlands”), itself modelled on Dutch de Verenigde Nederlanden (“the United Netherlands”).
By surface analysis, de (“the”) + forente (“united”) + Nederlandene (“the Low Countries”), literally “the United Low Countries”.
